body: On November 11, 2011, Bethesda Game Studios releases The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim on PC, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in North America and Europe. The date 11/11/11 becomes part of the memory of the launch itself. Skyrim lowers many traditional role-playing barriers: it does not ask players to choose a class immediately, lets skills grow through use and distributes quests, ruins and detours across a landscape made readable by large landmarks. Dragons enter the world as a mobile threat and Shouts turn learned words into powers. The Nordic setting, made of wood, stone, mist and mountains, supports a more physical sense of travel than Oblivion. The game's long life, also fueled by mods and rereleases, shows how that open structure became a cultural platform as well as an adventure.

Skyrim orients the player even when the map is not open. The Throat of the World dominates the horizon, cities, fortresses and ruins create recognizable silhouettes, and roads bend around mountains that often force the route to be reconsidered. This geography makes exploration less abstract: seeing a place in the distance creates a promise, but reaching it requires reading altitude, passages and detours. Bethesda describes the freedom to choose a direction as a fundamental part of The Elder Scrolls experience. Skyrim reinforces this idea through a landscape more vertical and severe than Cyrodiil. The compass also helps without completely replacing observation, because many points of interest are first perceived as silhouettes or openings in rock. The open world thus functions as a network of visual invitations, continually interrupting whatever objective the player had chosen only minutes earlier.

Skyrim removes the initial choice of a rigid class and ties much of character growth to using skills. Fighting one-handed, smithing, lockpicking, casting spells or moving stealthily advances different abilities; when the character levels up, perks then allow specialization in what is actually being used. The structure reduces the distance between behavior and the character sheet. Players do not need to know in advance what role they will want to perform for hours: they can change habits and let the build emerge from experience. Bethesda presents this freedom as one of the game's central principles. The system retains RPG numbers and choices, but distributes them through repeated, readable actions. This makes progression especially suited to the open world, because a detour can also become a learning opportunity: exploring a mine, forging a weapon and using it all belong to the same path of growth.

Dragons are not merely spectacular antagonists: they connect combat, exploration and progression. After absorbing a dragon soul, the Dragonborn can use words of the Dragon Language learned from Word Walls. Each Shout is composed of several words, and discovering new syllables encourages the search for tombs, mountains and ruins. Power therefore arises from two different activities, exploring and confronting creatures, which must come together before producing a complete result. Dragon encounters can also happen in open spaces and disrupt an ordinary journey, suddenly turning a village or valley into a battlefield. Bethesda thus uses the narrative theme of the Dragonborn as a systemic structure. Speaking the language of dragons is not a privilege described in a scene: it is a gameplay verb with cooldowns, variants and spatial consequences.

Skyrim's ruins must support two functions at once: offer a readable route and suggest who built, inhabited or violated them. Nordic tombs, forts, caves and Dwemer complexes use different materials, traps, bodies, objects and architecture to establish their character before any text intervenes. Many side stories emerge from journals and notes, but the arrangement of space continues to speak even to players who do not read them. Shortcuts that open near the entrance often prevent long backtracking, while larger rooms prepare encounters or rewards. The result is a form of storytelling woven into level design: advancing means interpreting signs and expectations as well as looking for the next enemy. In a game this large, such variety is essential for exploration to remain discovery rather than a simple succession of map markers.

Skyrim's art direction begins with a rough North built more from materials and wear than decoration. Bethesda has shown how concept artists and modelers translate sketches of armor, creatures and architecture into objects intended for the game world. Carved wood, iron, fur, stone and Nordic motifs form a coherent vocabulary that distinguishes cities and factions without turning them into isolated theme parks. The process from concept to character matters because it reveals how much visual identity depends on decisions repeated across hundreds of assets. A helmet, a door or a tavern must belong to the same cultural climate while performing different functions. The technical limits of the generation also require strong silhouettes and immediately recognizable materials. Skyrim therefore builds an imagery that remained identifiable through many rereleases because coherence comes before the sheer quantity of detail.

Skyrim quickly becomes one of the great laboratories of mod culture on PC. With the Creation Kit, the community can intervene in quests, spaces, rules, interfaces, objects and characters, producing fixes, transformations and almost autonomous works. Bethesda later brings mod support to console editions as well, with different limitations depending on the platform. This openness changes the relationship between audience and work: an important part of Skyrim's life is no longer organized only by the studio, but by thousands of authors building on the same foundation. Tenth-anniversary celebrations explicitly acknowledge the community's role in keeping the game alive. Longevity therefore depends on more than official rereleases. It also depends on Skyrim offering a world modular enough to be corrected, expanded and reinterpreted without immediately losing its identity.

old_entry.title: Minecraft
old_entry.subtitle: A world becomes a set of materials
old_entry.summary: Mining, making and sharing turn a landscape into an ongoing collective project.
body: On May 17, 2009 Markus Persson made public an early version of Cave Game, the project that would become Minecraft. The prototype was still far from the universe of systems, creatures and communities now associated with it, but already contained the decisive idea: terrain is made of blocks that players can remove and place elsewhere. From that gesture would grow survival, architecture, logic circuits, servers and educational practices. Minecraft became enormous because it does not prescribe one goal. It offers a common material from which different people can invent different purposes.

Minecraft's early strength lies in the consistency of the block. Dirt, stone, wood and many other materials share a common measure that can be understood without long manuals. Breaking and placing are simple actions, yet their combination produces shelters, stairs, bridges, monuments and mistakes. The world is not presented as untouchable scenery. Almost every surface invites interpretation as a resource. This uniformity makes the system accessible while remaining open enough to support constructions of unpredictable complexity.

Minecraft does not need a written mission to teach urgency. The sun falls, darkness increases and hostile creatures suddenly make shelter important. The day-night cycle turns time into natural pressure and provides an early reason to gather materials. Surviving the night teaches that building is not only decoration. Later, players can ignore, dominate or automate many threats, but the first improvised house remains a memorable lesson about the relationship between environment and safety.

The crafting table converts gathered materials into tools, blocks and objects through recipes. Progression is not a list of abstract levels but a network of transformations. Wood becomes planks, planks become sticks and sticks enter tools that allow access to other materials. This chain makes the world's economy understandable because every step leaves a visible trace. Learning Minecraft often means remembering relationships among things rather than isolated statistics. Knowledge of recipes becomes a form of competence shared between game and community.
Minecraft was available in public development before the release of version 1.0 in 2011. Its blocks give terrain a consistent grammar: an object can be removed, carried and placed somewhere else.

The game grew from Markus Persson's early work into a wider Mojang production and a vast player culture. Buildings, servers, technical contraptions, lessons and videos extend its history far beyond one official set of objectives.

editorial_features.title: A world made together
body: In his February 2011 postmortem, Markus Persson describes players finding purposes in Minecraft that he had not originally prioritized. Free building from an early engine test became Creative mode because people continued to enjoy it. He also recalls changing his mind about custom textures after seeing a player made Portal server. The work arriving from outside the studio could make an argument through something playable. A modification showed what an option might accomplish more directly than a request for another feature alone could do.

Persson's account also identifies the cost of postponing multiplayer during a rewrite. New systems had accumulated assumptions about a single player, mixing parts of their rules with the code that drew them. Moving inventory to the server required substantial further work. Shared building therefore depended on less visible agreements beneath the blocks. The software had to determine which state belonged to everyone, rather than letting each screen behave like a complete private world. His postmortem describes a change toward testing new features in both modes earlier.

Jens Bergensten explains another shared rule in a 2016 interview: building remains an action involving one block at a time. An efficient editor could place more at once, but he wanted another person to understand a construction as it happened. Two builders could also work faster together. The limit gives collaboration an immediately visible form. Someone can follow the next placement, contribute a neighbouring piece and recognize how an unfinished structure is becoming a larger plan through actions that remain small enough to read.

A 2017 snapshot announcement shows another scale of improvement. Creative players could save and reload toolbars, preserving a chosen set of materials instead of repeatedly assembling it. The same experimental release introduced concrete, concrete powder and glazed terracotta. The publication asks players to report bugs and protect their worlds before testing. New building possibilities arrived alongside a practical testing routine. A public update could supply tools for making things while also inviting the audience to help discover how those tools behaved outside the development team's own examples.

Almost every surface invites interpretation as a resource. This uniformity makes the system accessible while remaining open enough to support constructions of unpredictable complexity. Minecraft does not need a written mission to teach urgency. The sun falls, darkness increases and hostile creatures suddenly make shelter important. Wood becomes planks, planks become sticks and sticks enter tools that allow access to other materials. This chain makes the world's economy understandable because every step leaves a visible trace. Learning Minecraft often means remembering relationships among things rather than isolated statistics. Knowledge of recipes becomes a form of competence shared between game and community. The choice works because it is repeated and tested. In Minecraft, crafting, recipes and progression gains value over time, turning a local solution into a stable part of how the game is remembered.

new_entry.title: Minecraft
new_entry.subtitle: A world becomes a set of materials
new_entry.summary: Mining, making and sharing turn a landscape into an ongoing collective project.
body: On May 17, 2009 Markus Persson made public an early version of Minecraft, the project previously called Cave Game. The prototype was still far from the universe of systems, creatures and communities now associated with it, but already contained the decisive idea: terrain is made of blocks that players can remove and place elsewhere. From that gesture would grow survival, architecture, logic circuits, servers and educational practices. Minecraft became enormous because it does not prescribe one goal. It offers a common material from which different people can invent different purposes.

Minecraft's early strength lies in the consistency of the block. Dirt, stone, wood and many other materials share a common measure that can be understood without long manuals. Breaking and placing are simple actions, yet their combination produces shelters, stairs, bridges, monuments and mistakes. The world is not presented as untouchable scenery. Almost every surface invites interpretation as a resource. This uniformity makes the system accessible while remaining open enough to support constructions of unpredictable complexity.

Minecraft does not need a written mission to teach urgency. The sun falls, darkness increases and hostile creatures suddenly make shelter important. The day-night cycle turns time into natural pressure and provides an early reason to gather materials. Surviving the night teaches that building is not only decoration. Later, players can ignore, dominate or automate many threats, but the first improvised house remains a memorable lesson about the relationship between environment and safety.

The crafting table converts gathered materials into tools, blocks and objects through recipes. Progression is not a list of abstract levels but a network of transformations. Wood becomes planks, planks become sticks and sticks enter tools that allow access to other materials. This chain makes the world's economy understandable because every step leaves a visible trace. Learning Minecraft often means remembering relationships among things rather than isolated statistics. Knowledge of recipes becomes a form of competence shared between game and community.

Minecraft was available in public development before the release of version 1.0 in 2011. Its blocks give terrain a consistent grammar: an object can be removed, carried and placed somewhere else. The game grew from Markus Persson's early work into a wider Mojang production and a vast player culture. Buildings, servers, technical contraptions, lessons and videos extend its history far beyond one official set of objectives.

editorial_features.title: A world made together
editorial_features.summary: Players helped shape Minecraft's creative building, custom textures and multiplayer tools.
body: In his February 2011 postmortem, Markus Persson describes players finding purposes in Minecraft that he had not originally prioritized. Free building from an early engine test became Creative mode because people continued to enjoy it. He also recalls changing his mind about custom textures after seeing a player made Portal server. The work arriving from outside the studio could make an argument through something playable. A modification showed what an option might accomplish more directly than a request for another feature alone could do.

Persson's account also identifies the cost of postponing multiplayer during a rewrite. New systems had accumulated assumptions about a single player, mixing parts of their rules with the code that drew them. Moving inventory to the server required substantial further work. Shared building therefore depended on less visible agreements beneath the blocks. The software had to determine which state belonged to everyone, rather than letting each screen behave like a complete private world. His postmortem describes a change toward testing new features in both modes earlier.

Jens Bergensten explains another shared rule in a 2016 interview: building remains an action involving one block at a time. An efficient editor could place more at once, but he wanted another person to understand a construction as it happened. Two builders could also work faster together. The limit gives collaboration an immediately visible form. Someone can follow the next placement, contribute a neighbouring piece and recognize how an unfinished structure is becoming a larger plan through actions that remain small enough to read.

A 2017 snapshot announcement shows another scale of improvement. Creative players could save and reload toolbars, preserving a chosen set of materials instead of repeatedly assembling it. The same experimental release introduced concrete, concrete powder and glazed terracotta. The publication asks players to report bugs and protect their worlds before testing. New building possibilities arrived alongside a practical testing routine. A public update could supply tools for making things while also inviting the audience to help discover how those tools behaved outside the development team's own examples.
story_headings: Players inspire Creative mode and custom textures
Building one block at a time

old_entry.title: Saints Row: The Third
old_entry.summary: Saints Row: The Third is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Volition and published by THQ.
body: Saints Row: The Third is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Volition and published by THQ. It is the sequel to 2008's Saints Row 2 and the third installment in the Saints Row series. It was released on November 15, 2011, for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360, and May 10, 2019, for the Nintendo Switch. A remastered version of the game, titled Saints Row: The Third Remastered, was released by Deep Silver on May 22, 2020, for the PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One, March 5, 2021, for Stadia, May 25, 2021, for the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, and July 29, 2021, for Luna, and was announced for release on Android, iOS and iPadOS by Feral Interactive for October 29, 2026.

The game is set in the fictional city of Steelport and continues the story of the 3rd Street Saints, once again placing players in the role of the gang's leader, who is fully customizable. Years after the events of Saints Row 2, the Saints have grown from their humble origins as a street gang into a large media and consumer empire with their own brand, while many of the gang's members have become celebrities and pop culture icons. After being stranded in Steelport, which is firmly ruled by an international crime organization known as the Syndicate, the Saints must rebuild their forces once more to take over the city and defeat the Syndicate, as well as S.T.A.G., a violent paramilitary contracted with restoring order to Steelport.

Development of Saints Row: The Third began in late 2008, shortly after the release of Saints Row 2. There was high staff turnover from the previous Saints Row team, with only one-fifth of the final 100-person staff having worked on a previous title in the series. They aimed to improve on the series by giving the game a coherent tone, and found it in films such as Hot Fuzz and the game's signature sex toy bat.

The game received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its general zaniness and customization options. Criticism was aimed at the new setting, which many critics felt was flat and underdeveloped compared to the previous games' Stilwater, and the lackluster humor. On the contrary, others thought the game perfected the Saints Row formula. It was a nominee for Best Narrative at the 2012 Game Developers Conference, an IGN Editor's Choice, and a recipient of perfect scores from GamesRadar and G4. A complete edition including the three downloadable content packs was released in 2012, and its planned Enter the Dominatrix expansion became the game's sequel, Saints Row IV, released in 2013.

old_entry.title: Nobuo Uematsu: placing the music
old_entry.summary: Music changes through tools and implementation.
body: Uematsu remembered entering Famicom music note by note, with instructions for pitch, length and repetition. Writing did not finish when a melody existed in his head: it still had to become information a program could play. He also experimented with slightly different frequencies and timing between matching lines to create a shimmering sound. The desired expression emerged from those adjustments. His account describes a composer working inside an electronic instrument, testing how a small difference in execution could make a familiar phrase feel less rigid.

Moving to the Super Famicom meant learning with another person. Uematsu recalled being paired with a sound programmer and spending their days sampling and testing tones together. The larger palette did not arrive as a ready orchestra whose colours could simply be selected. Somebody had to prepare the sounds and discover how they behaved. His enthusiasm for adding drum sounds belongs inside that shared experiment. The change was musical and organisational at once: new resources created possibilities, while a collaboration made those possibilities usable in practice.

The Last Story presented a different problem: a finished composition could become material for someone else's editing. In Nintendo's 2011 conversation, Uematsu welcomed battle music being separated into sections rather than always playing its full length. Visiting the development team surprised him because the music had acquired uses he had not anticipated. The account shifts attention from composing a tune to placing it within an action. The resulting experience depended on the person implementing the music as well as the person who had written it.

Uematsu proposed an audio director who would judge the whole sound world without having created every component. Ambient noise, musical placement and balance needed attention together. He, Sakaguchi and the audio implementer had exchanged detailed emails, and working apart sometimes made intentions difficult to explain. He discussed this proposal with Nintendo's Satoru Iwata while considering how collaborators could hear their combined work. It identifies the distance between delivering music and hearing a game: someone must assess how separate contributions meet when a player actually encounters them.

old_entry.title: Mario Kart 7
old_entry.summary: Mario Kart 7 is a 2011 kart racing game developed by Nintendo EAD in cooperation with Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS.
body: Mario Kart 7 is a 2011 kart racing game developed by Nintendo EAD in cooperation with Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS. In Mario Kart 7, the player takes control of one of seventeen Mario series characters, who participate in races on various Mario-themed race tracks using specialized items to hinder opponents or gain advantages. In single player mode, players can race against computer-controlled characters in 8 multi-race cups consisting of 32 tracks (4 in each cup) over three difficulty levels. Alternatively, players can race against the clock in a Time Trial mode.

New additions to Mario Kart 7 include hang-gliding attachments for karts (which introduced aerial sections to race tracks for the first time in the series), the ability to drive in first person, gyro controls, and the ability to customize the vehicles' builds. Additionally, Mario Kart 7 supports both local and online multiplayer through Nintendo Network for up to eight players. The ability to play online was discontinued on April 8, 2024, along with Nintendo Network as a whole.

Development of Mario Kart 7 began in early 2010 as a port of Mario Kart Wii. Producer Hideki Konno said that completing the game was an "act of emergency" due to low 3DS sales at that time and because of the very few staff involved in its development. In the end, Retro Studios was involved in the development of the retro tracks (tracks from prior games in the series). Mario Kart 7 received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its innovations, race tracks, and gyro control option. The game has won several awards and was a commercial success, becoming the best-selling game on the Nintendo 3DS with nearly 19 million copies sold.

new_entry.title: Mario Kart 7
new_entry.summary: Mario Kart 7 is a 2011 kart racing game developed by Nintendo EAD in cooperation with Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS.
body: Mario Kart 7 is a 2011 kart racing game developed by Nintendo EAD in cooperation with Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS. In Mario Kart 7, the player takes control of one of seventeen Mario series characters, who participate in races on various Mario-themed race tracks using specialized items to hinder opponents or gain advantages. In single player mode, players can race against computer-controlled characters in 8 multi-race cups consisting of 32 tracks (4 in each cup) over three difficulty levels. Alternatively, players can race against the clock in a Time Trial mode.

New additions to Mario Kart 7 include hang-gliding attachments for karts (which introduced aerial sections to race tracks for the first time in the series), the ability to drive in first person, gyro controls, and the ability to customize the vehicles' builds. Additionally, Mario Kart 7 supports both local and online multiplayer through Nintendo Network for up to eight players. The ability to play online was discontinued on April 8, 2024, along with Nintendo Network as a whole.

Development of Mario Kart 7 began in early 2010 as a port of Mario Kart Wii. Producer Hideki Konno said that completing the game was an "act of emergency" due to low 3DS sales at that time and because of the very few staff involved in its development. In the end, Retro Studios was involved in the development of the retro tracks (tracks from prior games in the series). Mario Kart 7 received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its innovations, race tracks, and gyro control option. The game has won several awards and was a commercial success, becoming the best-selling game on the Nintendo 3DS with nearly 19 million copies sold.
story_headings: Developing with Retro Studios and success on 3DS

old_entry.title: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword
old_entry.summary: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword is a 2011 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii.
body: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword is a 2011 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii. A mainline entry in The Legend of Zelda series, Skyward Sword is the first game in the Zelda timeline, and details the origins of the Triforce and the Master Sword. The aeries main protagonist Link, a resident of a floating town called Skyloft, sets out to rescue his childhood friend Zelda after she is kidnapped and brought to the abandoned lands below the clouds. As Link, players navigate Skyloft and the lands below it, completing quests that advance the story and solving environmental and dungeon-based puzzles. The mechanics and combat, the latter focusing on attacking and blocking with sword and shield, are reliant on the Wii MotionPlus peripheral.

Development took around five years, beginning after the release of Twilight Princess in 2006. Multiple earlier Zelda games influenced the developers, including Twilight Princess, Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask. Many aspects of the game's overworld and gameplay were designed to streamline and populate the experience for players. The art style was influenced by the work of impressionist and post-impressionist painters, including Paul Cézanne. The implementation of Wii MotionPlus proved problematic for the developers, to the point where it was nearly discarded. It was the first Zelda game to use a live orchestra for the majority of its tracks, with music composed by a team led by Hajime Wakai and supervised by Koji Kondo.

Announced in 2009, Skyward Sword was planned for release in 2010 but was delayed to November 2011 to further refine and expand it. It was a critical and commercial success, receiving perfect scores from multiple journalistic sites, winning and receiving nominations for numerous industry and journalist awards, and selling over three million copies worldwide. However, critics and series fans expressed criticism over its excessive linearity and backtracking, its motion controls, a general lack of innovation in the gameplay and were divided on its narrative choices. Feedback on the game later influenced the development of future Zelda games, including A Link Between Worlds and the next entry for home consoles Breath of the Wild.

A high-definition remaster of the game, The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD, was co-developed by Tantalus Media and released for the Nintendo Switch in July 2021. As of March 2022, the remaster had sold nearly 4 million units worldwide.

new_entry.title: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword
new_entry.summary: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword is a 2011 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii.
body: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword is a 2011 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii. A mainline entry in The Legend of Zelda series, Skyward Sword is the first game in the Zelda timeline, and details the origins of the Triforce and the Master Sword. The series' main protagonist Link, a resident of a floating town called Skyloft, sets out to rescue his childhood friend Zelda after she is kidnapped and brought to the abandoned lands below the clouds. As Link, players navigate Skyloft and the lands below it, completing quests that advance the story and solving environmental and dungeon-based puzzles. The mechanics and combat, the latter focusing on attacking and blocking with sword and shield, are reliant on the Wii MotionPlus peripheral.

Development took around five years, beginning after the release of Twilight Princess in 2006. Multiple earlier Zelda games influenced the developers, including Twilight Princess, Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask. Many aspects of the game's overworld and gameplay were designed to streamline and populate the experience for players. The art style was influenced by the work of impressionist and post-impressionist painters, including Paul Cézanne. The implementation of Wii MotionPlus proved problematic for the developers, to the point where it was nearly discarded. It was the first Zelda game to use a live orchestra for the majority of its tracks, with music composed by a team led by Hajime Wakai and supervised by Koji Kondo.

Announced in 2009, Skyward Sword was planned for release in 2010 but was delayed to November 2011 to further refine and expand it. It was a critical and commercial success, receiving perfect scores from multiple journalistic sites, winning and receiving nominations for numerous industry and journalist awards, and selling over three million copies worldwide. However, critics and series fans expressed criticism over its excessive linearity and backtracking, its motion controls, a general lack of innovation in the gameplay and were divided on its narrative choices. Feedback on the game later influenced the development of future Zelda games, including A Link Between Worlds and the next entry for home consoles Breath of the Wild.

A high-definition remaster of the game, The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD, was co-developed by Tantalus Media and released for the Nintendo Switch in July 2021. As of March 2022, the remaster had sold nearly 4 million units worldwide.
story_headings: Link between Skyloft and the world below
Five years of development and the MotionPlus challenge
Success, criticism and influence on later games

body: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword is a 2011 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii. A mainline entry in The Legend of Zelda series, Skyward Sword is the first game in the Zelda timeline, and details the origins of the Triforce and the Master Sword. The aeries main protagonist Link, a resident of a floating town called Skyloft, sets out to rescue his childhood friend Zelda after she is kidnapped and brought to the abandoned lands below the clouds. As Link, players navigate Skyloft and the lands below it, completing quests that advance the story and solving environmental and dungeon-based puzzles. The mechanics and combat, the latter focusing on attacking and blocking with sword and shield, are reliant on the Wii MotionPlus peripheral.

Development took around five years, beginning after the release of Twilight Princess in 2006. Multiple earlier Zelda games influenced the developers, including Twilight Princess, Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask. Many aspects of the game's overworld and gameplay were designed to streamline and populate the experience for players. The art style was influenced by the work of impressionist and post-impressionist painters, including Paul Cézanne. The implementation of Wii MotionPlus proved problematic for the developers, to the point where it was nearly discarded. It was the first Zelda game to use a live orchestra for the majority of its tracks, with music composed by a team led by Hajime Wakai and supervised by Koji Kondo.

Announced in 2009, Skyward Sword was planned for release in 2010 but was delayed to November 2011 to further refine and expand it. It was a critical and commercial success, receiving perfect scores from multiple journalistic sites, winning and receiving nominations for numerous industry and journalist awards, and selling over three million copies worldwide. However, critics and series fans expressed criticism over its excessive linearity and backtracking, its motion controls, a general lack of innovation in the gameplay and were divided on its narrative choices. Feedback on the game later influenced the development of future Zelda games, including A Link Between Worlds and the next entry for home consoles Breath of the Wild.

A high-definition remaster of the game, The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD, was co-developed by Tantalus Media and released for the Nintendo Switch in July 2021. As of March 2022, the remaster had sold nearly 4 million units worldwide.

old_entry.title: Final Fantasy XIII-2
old_entry.summary: Final Fantasy XIII-2 is a 2011 role-playing video game developed and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360.
body: Final Fantasy XIII-2 is a 2011 role-playing video game developed and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. It was released in 2011 in Japan and 2012 in North America and PAL regions, and was ported to Windows in 2014. XIII-2 is a direct sequel to the 2009 role-playing game Final Fantasy XIII and part of the Fabula Nova Crystallis subseries. It includes modified features from the previous game, including fast-paced combat and a customizable "Paradigm" system to control which abilities are used by the characters, and adds a new system that allows monsters to be captured and used in battle. The game's plot features a heavy time travel element, allowing the player to jump between different times at the same location or different places at the same time. Lightning, the protagonist of the original game, has disappeared into an unknown world. Her younger sister Serah Farron and Noel Kreiss journey through time in an attempt to find her.

Development of Final Fantasy XIII-2 began in early 2010 and lasted about one and a half years. The game was unveiled at the Square Enix 1st Production Department Premier in January 2011. Many of the key designers remained in their roles from the previous game, and developer tri-Ace was hired to help with the game's design, art, and programming. The development team wanted to exceed Final Fantasy XIII in every aspect while making the story's tone more dark and mysterious than the previous game. The game builds upon the Paradigm Shift battle system used in XIII and includes a less linear overall design.

Final Fantasy XIII-2 received critical acclaim in Japan and generally positive reviews from Western video game journalists. Though praised for its gameplay, lack of linearity, and graphics, the game's story was criticized as weak and confusing. The game was the fifth-best selling game of 2011 in Japan, and sold 3.1 million copies worldwide by January 2013. A sequel, Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII, was released in 2013 in Japan and 2014 worldwide.

The game was added to Xbox One backward compatibility along with its predecessor and sequel in November 2018. It is also Xbox One X Enhanced, allowing it to display in 4K Ultra HD. In November 2021, support for FPS Boost on Xbox Series X/S was added allowing it to run at 60 frames per second.

A sequel, Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII, was released in 2013 in Japan and 2014 worldwide.

The game was added to Xbox One backward compatibility along with its predecessor and sequel in November 2018. It is also Xbox One X Enhanced, allowing it to display in 4K Ultra HD. In November 2021, support for FPS Boost on Xbox Series X/S was added allowing it to run at 60 frames per second.

old_entry.title: Uncharted: Golden Abyss
old_entry.summary: Uncharted: Golden Abyss is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Bend Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation Vita.
body: Uncharted: Golden Abyss is a 2011 action-adventure game developed by Bend Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation Vita. A spin-off of Naughty Dog's Uncharted series, the game was released as a launch title for the console. Golden Abyss is a prequel to the series, taking place before the events of Uncharted: Drake's Fortune. The story revolves around adventurer-treasure hunter Nathan Drake as he becomes involved in a search for the lost city of Quivira and is aided by fellow treasure hunter Marisa Chase. Gameplay combines action-adventure with platforming elements, with players solving puzzles and fighting enemies using cover-based third-person shooting.

Concept work for Golden Abyss began in 2007, when Sony asked Bend Studio to develop a new Uncharted as a console launch title. Due to the changing specifications of the Vita, much of the early development was done using PlayStation 3 hardware. The entire project was overseen by original developer Naughty Dog, with Bend Studio receiving assets from the first two Uncharted titles and getting access to their motion capture facilities. John Garvin was both director and scriptwriter, the latter under the supervision of main series writer Amy Hennig. Hennig also ensured the return of Nolan North as Drake and Richard McGonagle as Sully.

The game was revealed in January 2011 alongside the Vita. Golden Abyss debuted to strong sales and generally positive critical reception. Journalists praised its graphics, voice performances, and recreation of Uncharted gameplay on the platform. Criticism focused on its storyline and implementation of Vita-specific controls. To date, the game remains exclusive to the platform, as it was left out of the PlayStation 4's Uncharted: The Nathan Drake Collection due to the standalone nature of its narrative.

new_entry.title: Ridge Racer
new_entry.summary: Ridge Racer, originally named Ridge Racer Vita, is a 2011 racing video game published by Namco Bandai Games for the PlayStation Vita as a launch title, originally on 17 December 2011 in Japan, and internationally from February 2012.
body: Ridge Racer, originally named Ridge Racer Vita, is a 2011 racing video game published by Namco Bandai Games for the PlayStation Vita as a launch title, originally on 17 December 2011 in Japan, and internationally from February 2012. It is the 5th handheld game in the Ridge Racer series and the first on a Sony platform since 2006's Ridge Racer 2. It was the first and only game in the series developed by Cellius. The game continues the Ridge Racer tradition of arcade racing and supports single-player as well as local and Wi-Fi multiplayer games. Upon release, Ridge Racer was mostly panned by video game critics due to the lack of a career mode and particularly the lack of content, with much of it locked as paid downloadable content.

It is an arcade-style racing game with high speed drifting. Players can start drifts around corners and steer it to maintain their speed, which charges the car's nitro. This game features slipstreaming which allows players to gain speed by following closely behind opponents. The main game modes are Spot Race, Time Attack and World Race. It has an online mode for up to 8 players and local races over LAN or Wi-Fi. Credits earned from the races can be used to purchase car upgrades.

The Hornet from Sega's Daytona USA makes a cameo appearance as available DLC, as well as an exclusive song (with lyrics by Takenobu Mitsuyoshi) and course inspired by both franchises. Other cameos include cars with paint schemes derived from The Idolmaster, as well as DoCoMO and Pac-Man-themed versions of the Kamata SYNCi, the game's cover car. The DoCoMo and Idolmaster cars are not available outside Japan. Other downloadable content include new cars and courses, as well as music tracks from previous entries in the franchise.
